fields.h1: Build a Teacher Evaluation Survey for Students and Peers
fields.hero_description: Build a teacher evaluation survey students answer one question at a time, with results by class in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Each Survey Shows the Teacher
fields.features_subheading: Students answer one question per screen, and each class's results reach the teacher with no names attached.
fields.feature_1:
Results split by class or block

Ask which period, block, or section a student is in, and every chart can split on it. A teacher with five classes sees each one on its own line, next to the average for all of them.
fields.feature_2:
Picture scales for early grades

Swap the words for three faces on any question, and young students tap the face that fits while the teacher reads aloud. Each face is saved as a number and charts like any scale.
fields.feature_3:
Anonymous from the first screen

Leave student names and emails off, and say so before question 1. Set a minimum, such as 5 answers, and any class under it stays out of the results until more students respond.
fields.feature_4:
One question per screen

Students move through the survey one question at a time on a phone or a classroom laptop. A 10-question survey fits the last minutes of a lesson, and nobody scrolls a long page.
fields.feature_5:
A low score goes to the teacher first

Email the teacher when a class falls below the score you set on any question. Send a department head only the count of surveys finished, and keep the comments with the teacher.
fields.feature_6:
The answers and the code stay yours

Every answer is a row in a database the school owns, with no cap on responses. On paid plans, export the full survey app to your GitHub repository and change it for next term.

fields.usecase_heading: Who Answers the Survey, and Who Reads It
fields.tab_content_1:
Block E splits on pace, with 12 of 26 agreeing

Rennick Hale teaches chemistry at Alder Crest High School and runs his own survey in every block at mid-semester. This fall, 131 students answered. In 4 blocks, at least 75% agreed that the pace of the class worked for them. Block E split, with 12 of 26 agreeing, and he spread its next lab across 2 days.
fields.tab_content_2:
Done early and unsure: 7 of 22 second graders

Odette Varga reads each question aloud to her 22 second graders at Wrenfield Elementary, and each child picks a face on a classroom laptop: a smile, a straight face, or a frown. Asked whether they know what to do once their work is done, 7 of 22 picked the frown. She posted a choice board the next week.
fields.tab_content_3:
Peer visit notes stay with each teacher observed

Halden Middle School pairs its teachers for 20-minute peer visits each quarter. The observer fills in a short form on a phone, and the app emails the notes only to the teacher observed. Gwen Ashby got Tomas Reyes's notes on her grade 7 science class. The principal sees one number: 16 of 16 visits done.
fields.tab_content_4:
One class averages 3.2 on speaking time

Harborline Adult School has its evening English learners rate their instructor after each 8-week term. This term, 112 learners answered. On getting time to speak in class, 3 instructors averaged 4.3 or higher out of 5. Teo Brennan's class averaged 3.2, and director Amara Lindqvist is planning speaking drills with him.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Teacher Evaluation Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to write a teacher evaluation survey that fits the age group and ends with students hearing what changed.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Match the scale to the age
fields.howto_step_1_des: Settle who sees the answers before you write a question: the teacher alone, an instructional coach, or the principal. Tell students on the first screen who will read their answers, and keep that promise the same every term so results stay comparable.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write statements about things a student sees in class every week, such as whether the teacher checks that everyone followed before moving on or returns graded work within a week. Leave out personality and appearance, and ask about one thing per statement.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Use faces for children who cannot yet read the questions, and a five-point agree scale once students read on their own. Read every question aloud to young students, and word each question the same way in every class you survey.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Run the survey during the last 10 minutes of a lesson, not as homework. Step away from the screens while students answer, or ask a colleague to share the link, and give students who were absent a second day to finish.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Keep names and student ID numbers off the survey, and hold back results for any class with fewer than 5 answers. In a small class, skip questions about age or background that could point to one student, and say on screen that you did.
fields.howto_step_6_des: End with one open question, such as what the teacher should keep doing next term. Read the comments next to the scores for the same class, and look for the unit or the assignment a low rating on pace or clarity points to.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Within 2 weeks, tell each class what the survey showed and one thing you will change, such as a slower lab schedule. Open the next survey by naming that change before question 1, and ask whether students noticed it.

faq_plan.q: What is a teacher evaluation survey?
faq_plan.a: A teacher evaluation survey is a short questionnaire in which students, or a colleague who watched a lesson, rate how a teacher's class works for them. Its statements cover the pace, how clearly steps are explained, and how quickly graded work comes back. The answers show the teacher what to keep and what to change.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a teacher evaluation survey?
faq_plan.a: Decide who will read the results, then write statements about what students see in class, on a scale that suits their age. With Emergent's AI survey builder, you describe the survey in a sentence or two, and Emergent builds the questions, the results view, and the database behind them. Test it with a few students before the whole class takes it.

faq_plan.q: What teacher evaluation survey questions should students answer?
faq_plan.a: Ask about things students see in class every week. Good teacher evaluation survey questions include: The teacher explains a step again when I ask. I get graded work back in time to use the feedback. The pace of this class works for me. I can ask for help without feeling embarrassed. Make the last question open-ended and ask what should change next term.

faq_plan.q: Is there a teacher evaluation survey template I can adapt for my school?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Use one teacher evaluation survey template across your school, with the same statements in every class, and a teacher can compare blocks and terms side by side. Swap in faces for the early grades and leave the wording alone otherwise. To hear from families as well, run a separate parent survey instead of adding their questions to the student version.

faq_plan.q: Should a teacher evaluation survey be anonymous?
faq_plan.a: Yes, for students. Leave off names, emails and student ID numbers, and say so on the first screen. If a student wants a follow-up, add an optional last question that asks for a name, and keep the answers before it unlinked. Peer visit notes work the other way: the teacher should know who observed, so name the observer and keep the notes private.

faq_plan.q: How do you give a teacher evaluation survey to students who are still learning to read?
faq_plan.a: Read each question aloud and let students answer with pictures instead of words, such as happy and sad faces. Start with a practice question about something neutral, such as a favorite recess game, and keep the survey short. Emergent can build it as a one-question-per-screen flow from a prompt, with the faces large enough to tap.

faq_plan.q: Can a tutoring program with volunteer tutors use a teacher evaluation survey?
faq_plan.a: A tutoring program can use the same format. Learners, or parents of younger learners, rate statements about each tutor: whether sessions start on time, whether explanations make sense, and whether the learner feels more ready for class. To ask the tutors themselves how the role is going, send a separate volunteer survey.

faq_plan.q: When in the school year should students take a teacher evaluation survey?
faq_plan.a: Run it twice: at mid-semester, while there is time to change something for the same students, and again in the last weeks of the course. Skip the days right after a test comes back, and use the same statements both times. In an app Emergent builds, both rounds are stored in the school's own database, ready to compare.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a teacher evaluation survey have?
faq_plan.a: About 10 for middle and high school: one question for the class or block, 8 statements on a rating scale, and one open question. For students still learning to read, keep it to 5 or 6. There is no response cap in Emergent, so every class in the school can take the same survey.

faq_plan.q: Can a Sunday school run a teacher evaluation survey for its teachers?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Keep it short: ask students, or parents for the youngest classes, whether lessons are easy to follow and whether the class feels welcoming, and send the results only to the teacher and the program lead. To hear from the whole congregation about more than its classes, use a church survey instead.

plan.angle: The searcher wants teacher evaluation survey questions and a template. The ranking pages are question lists and generic survey templates that stop at the questions, written for one audience. This page shows four teacher evaluation surveys running with their numbers: a high school teacher's own mid-semester survey split by class period, a picture-scale survey for second graders, a peer observation form whose notes go only to the teacher observed, and an adult school rating each instructor at term end. The FAQ then covers the questions, anonymity, timing, length, young readers and volunteer or faith-based programs, and the how-to covers who reads the results and what students hear back.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Teacher Evaluation Survey for Students and Peers'; hero 'Build a teacher evaluation survey students answer one question at a time, with results by class in a database you own.' carries the primary and leads with Build; how-to description 'Seven steps to write a teacher evaluation survey that fits the age group and ends with students hearing what changed.'

intent.evidence: Searchers want questions and a template: FAQ 3 gives sample statements ('The teacher explains a step again when I ask.' 'The pace of this class works for me.'), FAQ 4 the template, FAQ 9 length, step 2 more statements, four worked surveys with results in the tabs, a 7-step how-to.

specificity.evidence: Classroom vocabulary: 'Block E split, with 12 of 26 agreeing', 'a choice board', 'returns graded work within a week', '20-minute peer visits each quarter', 'evening English learners'.

openers.evidence: Full-sentence openers: 'Rennick Hale teaches chemistry at Alder Crest High School...', 'Settle who sees the answers before you write a question...', 'Ask which period, block, or section a student is in...'.

craft.evidence: No sentence over 40 words; two ', so' endings, under the Q5 limit; FAQ 3's inline statement list is a note.

voice.evidence: Plain and specific: 'She posted a choice board the next week.', 'The principal sees one number: 16 of 16 visits done.' why_description triplet is a note.

truth.evidence: No statements of fact about law, third-party systems or standards (domain_sources empty and none needed: definitions, advice and fictional tab data only). Emergent claims map to prompt-build, database-owned, conversational, alerts, no-caps, code-export, free-start. Numbers agree: 27+25+28+25+26 = 131; 21/28 = 75% so 'at least 75%' holds for 4 blocks; 12/26 = 46%; 1 + 8 + 1 = 10 questions (FAQ 9, mockup, feature 4); minimum 5 answers in feature 3 and step 5; three faces in feature 2, tab 2 and the image.

distinct.evidence: Students and peers rating a teacher; distinct from course-evaluation-survey (courses and modules) and from parent, church and volunteer surveys, which FAQ 4, 7 and 10 hand off by link; no sibling primary in a heading.

faq.evidence: 10 questions, answer-first, no brand or file-format ask; hub link in item 2; sibling links parent survey (FAQ 4), volunteer survey (FAQ 7), church survey (FAQ 10) read naturally: 'To ask the tutors themselves how the role is going, send a separate volunteer survey.' / 'To hear from the whole congregation about more than its classes, use a church survey instead.' Both secondaries used; F9 lines in FAQ 6, 8, 9.
